description: NatGin Father-daughter duo from Barranquilla, Colombia, joining virtually to learn, build and have fun. Gino is a telecom engineer (2G–5G) into data analysis and AI agents; his co-pilot brings creativity and Unity game dev skills. We use Python, data visualization and prototyping. Looking for teammates in remote sensing/data science, UI/UX design, storytelling or video, and front-end dev. Remote, UTC-5, friendly and organized. Beginners welcome: curiosity beats experience. Message us!
summary:
Two Hands, One Moon is a free 3D browser game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a base at the Moon's south pole for seven days. You play in first person with only two hands, three water bags and two batteries, so every choice has a cost: the water that makes oxygen cannot also grow lettuce or shield the crew from radiation.

Four bars (Oxygen, Energy, Protection, Food) show how each decision plays out. Each day adds one new problem: growing lettuce, recycling urine into water, going outside for ice, a solar storm, an air leak, a day in shadow, and liftoff. If a bar runs out, a "Mission Failed" screen explains the chain of causes with a real NASA fact, and the player retries that day with one star less.

The game uses real open data. Solar storms and solar clouds are real events from NASA's DONKI; faster clouds give less time to reach the shelter. The radio delay comes from NASA SVS Dial-A-Moon. Water and urine tank levels come from ISS Live! telemetry. All data is labeled with the date it was checked, and sources are shown inside the game.

It matters because children do not just read about life support, shielding, power, food and communication delay. They feel the trade-offs with their own hands. It runs on phones and computers with no account or download, in English, Spanish and Japanese.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Two Hands, One Moon is a first-person 3D game. The player is the only astronaut awake in a small base at the Moon's south pole and must keep four bars alive for seven days: Oxygen, Energy, Protection and Food. Resources are physical objects you carry: water bags and batteries. You have two hands, so you can only carry two things at a time.

HOW IT WORKS

The same water bag can make oxygen, water the lettuce, or sit in the shelter wall as radiation shielding, but never all three. The same battery can run the air machine, the grow lamp or the radio. There is no safe choice without a cost.

Each day introduces one new idea so young players are not overloaded:

Day 1: air and power. Day 2: food, and recycling urine into water. Day 3: going outside for ice and cleaning dusty solar panels. Day 4: a solar storm. Day 5: an air leak. Day 6: a mountain blocks the Sun. Day 7: everything together, then liftoff.

Solar clouds arrive by surprise and the player must run to the shelter in time. Radiation protection never recovers: it is a budget for the whole mission.

When a bar runs out, a "Mission Failed" screen shows the chain of causes and a real NASA fact. The player repeats that day with one star less, so failing teaches without punishing. Stars (up to 21) and collectible cards of real solar events reward replaying. There are two difficulty levels, Normal and Extreme.

REAL DATA IN THE GAME

- Solar storms and solar clouds are real space weather events from NASA DONKI (October 16 to November 14, 2026). A faster real cloud gives the player fewer seconds of warning.

- The radio delay (1.35 seconds each way) and the fact that Earth sits just below the horizon at the south pole come from NASA SVS Dial-A-Moon.

- Starting water and urine tank levels come from public International Space Station telemetry (ISS Live!). The game says clearly that this is the Station, not the Moon.

- Lettuce growth and food facts come from NASA Veggie and the Canadian Space Agency.

All data is embedded and labeled "REAL DATA, checked on Nov 14, 2026". It is not presented as live. Sources are listed inside the game.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

A child finishes the game understanding real deep-space limits: water is recycled and shared between jobs, radiation exposure adds up, power is scarce in shadow, and talking to Earth takes time. It works for kids playing alone, with siblings or parents, and in classrooms.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Trade-offs are not menus or numbers to compare. They are objects in your hands. We tested earlier versions (a control panel, a tile map and a block world) with family members of different ages and found that reading and comparing numbers was boring, so we rebuilt the idea around carrying things.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Accessibility: runs in a browser on phones and computers, no account, no download, one small file. Short sentences, optional computer voice that reads the text, three languages (English, Spanish, Japanese).

- Cost: free to play and free to host.

- Honesty: real data is dated and labeled; simplifications are our own and the game is not a NASA product.

TOOLS

JavaScript, HTML and CSS, three.js for 3D, Web Speech API for voices, sound and music generated by code, Python scripts to collect the NASA data, Cloudflare Pages for hosting.

USE OF AI

AI tools helped write code, game text and translations. Voices are computer-generated by the browser. The game idea, design decisions and playtesting were done by the team.
